title: Proof on the claimant
hookLine: the burden of proof is on the claimant, the oath on the one who denies
tomorrow: you see something wrong and can't fix it. is doing nothing ever okay?

cards: A charger vanishes from the break room, and by lunch three people have quietly decided who took it. Nobody saw anything. Everyone just feels sure.
So, yesterday's question: money's gone, everyone knows who did it, are they right? Hadith thirty-three, from Ibn Abbas, starts with a warning.
If people were given whatever they claimed, some would claim the wealth and the blood of others. Then the rule: the proof is on the one who claims, and the oath on the one who denies.

teach.b: Start with the picture in the first half. If a claim alone were enough, anyone could point at your house and say, that's mine.
So the weight sits on the person making the claim: bring bayyinah, clear proof.

teach.h: THE OATH: THE ONE WHO DENIES.
teach.b: The one who denies doesn't have to prove his innocence. If there's no proof against him, he swears an oath, and that's the end of it.
The core of this is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; al-Nawawi gives the fuller wording. Here's the turn worth telling a friend: the accused isn't the one carrying the weight. The accuser is.
Then step outside the courtroom, because the accusations of an ordinary week happen in group chats, kitchens and break rooms, where a feeling of being sure does the work of a judge.
The Qur'an speaks to that room, in Pickthall's words: "Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime." So the question this hadith hands you, any day of the week, is simple.
Before the claim leaves your mouth: what's my proof? Not what do I feel, not who was nearby. What did I actually see?

how: In Islamic courts, the one who brings a claim must bring evidence; if there is none, the one who denies may swear an oath. Muslim teachers also apply the hadith to everyday accusations and suspicion.

games.q: what does “proof on the claimant” mean?
o: a rule that the richest party wins in court
whoever accuses must bring the evidence
whoever is accused must prove they're clean

s: under this hadith, the accused has to prove they're innocent
the opposite: the proof is on the one who claims; the one who denies only swears.
the hadith warns that if claims were enough, people would claim others' wealth and blood
that's why the weight sits on the claimant.
the Qur'an calls some suspicion a crime
Pickthall: "Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime."

games.q: your little brother says your sister broke his tablet. she says she didn't. nobody saw. you're the referee. what fits hadith thirty-three?
o: she was home all day, so it was probably her.
ground them both so nobody gets away with it.
ask him for evidence; if there isn't any, her word stands.
games.why: the proof is on the one who claims. without it, the one who denies is believed on her word.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've quietly blamed for something, big or small. Your wish: to be fair to them. The obstacle: that warm, certain feeling.
The plan: when I catch myself sure, I'll ask what I actually saw. Hold the plan through the sit, and let the person's face soften a little.

wordCard.voice: Proof on the claimant: the one who makes the claim brings the evidence; the one who denies only swears. Feeling sure isn't proof.

orig.note: Arabic: the proof is on the claimant. al-mudda'i is the one who makes a claim.

carryVoice: Pocket this: prove it first, before a guess becomes a verdict about somebody. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah, hadith 33 (Ibn Abbas; al-Bayhaqi, with its core in Bukhari and Muslim)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4552; Sahih Muslim 1711 (the oath is on the one claimed against)

sources.q: Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime.
